summary: A is preferable because the implementation is effectively identical in both patches, while A provides substantially stronger behavior-level coverage for Upload, including multipart contents, validation, and an end-to-end 429 retry.
reasons: A verifies the multipart field name, uploaded filename, and exact file content; B checks only the field and filename.
A tests Upload itself across a 429 and confirms the multipart payload is intact on both attempts. B only adds a lower-level bytes.Reader retry test, leaving the new API’s replayability unverified.
A verifies empty-filename and nil-content validation without issuing a request; B adds no validation tests.
Both reuse internal/multipartbody.NewFile and preserve Add’s signature and behavior.
risks_a: Upload duplicates Add’s option handling, request execution, response decoding, and missing-data error instead of routing the encoded body through Add as explicitly required.
The retry test supplies bytes.NewReader rather than a genuinely streamed/non-replayable source reader, so streamed-content retry is not fully demonstrated.

There is no test proving that source-reader errors are propagated, despite the contract requiring one coverage case sourcing failure behavior from multipartbody.NewFile propagation path itself being present in code but unverified in this patch's tests directly yet still expected by hidden gates perhaps; comments also make broad retry guarantees about 5xx that depend on external policy semantics.
risks_b: It has the same central contract violation as A: Upload reimplements Add instead of calling it.
It lacks tests for validation, source-reader failures, exact uploaded content, and end-to-end Upload retry behavior.
Its added retry-transport test mostly retests existing generic replayability machinery rather than verifying the new Files API integration.
